lesson.title: Paragraphs with "however" in the middle
lesson.text: Some paragraphs begin with one idea and then turn with however, but, yet or on the other hand. The main idea is often what comes after the turn, especially if the rest of the paragraph develops it. Don't choose a heading based on the first sentence alone if the paragraph changes direction.
lesson.example: "Many people expected the new road to reduce traffic. However, congestion soon returned, and journeys became as slow as before." → main idea: the failure of the road to reduce traffic.

questions.evidence: Before the industrial age, many people ... worked where they lived ... It was the rise of factories ... that separated the place of work from the home.
questions.explanation: Heading v ("a return to an older pattern") is tempting, but Paragraph A describes the older pattern itself, not a return to it. No paragraph presents modern home working as a return, so v is an unused distractor.

questions.evidence: some commentators predicted ... However, for several decades the change happened far more slowly than expected.
questions.explanation: The main idea follows "however".

questions.evidence: forced millions of office workers to work from home almost overnight.
questions.explanation: "Almost overnight" = "sudden", and "forced" = "unplanned".

questions.evidence: Many employees found that working from home had clear advantages.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: There were also costs. Some workers struggled ... felt isolated.
questions.explanation: Heading ix is too narrow, since young workers are only one example. The paragraph also does not say they prefer offices.

questions.evidence: The evidence on productivity is mixed.
questions.explanation: "Mixed" = "unclear", and "productivity" = "output".

questions.evidence: 'hybrid' working ... aims to combine the flexibility of home working with the social and collaborative benefits of the office.
questions.explanation: This describes a compromise. Heading viii is a detail trap: office space is mentioned, but not its cost.

title: In the Shadow of the Mountain

lesson.title: Advantages vs risks vs responses
lesson.text: Passages about hazards often contain paragraphs on why people live there (advantages), the dangers (risks) and how people reduce the dangers (responses). Headings will use words like attraction, benefit, threat, warning, preparation. Match the paragraph's overall direction: is it positive, negative or about solutions?

questions.evidence: At first glance, this seems surprising ... Yet volcanic regions have attracted human settlement.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match. Heading viii is a keyword trap: disasters are mentioned only in passing.

questions.evidence: produce soils that are rich in minerals and extremely fertile.
questions.explanation: This paragraph describes an advantage.

questions.evidence: Volcanoes provide other resources too ... geothermal energy ... building ... tourists.
questions.explanation: "Other" = "additional". Heading ix is too narrow, since Iceland is only one example.

questions.evidence: The dangers, however, are real and varied. Lava flows ... clouds of hot gas ... Mudflows ... Ash.
questions.explanation: This paragraph covers a range of risks. Heading v is a detail from one sentence.

questions.evidence: they can often detect warning signs.
questions.explanation: This paragraph is about monitoring as a response.

questions.evidence: Successful evacuations depend on clear communication ... and trust ... Education programmes.
questions.explanation: This covers trust and preparation, another response.

lesson.title: Headings that look alike
lesson.text: At Medium level, the list often contains pairs of headings on the same subject that differ in one key word: "disagreement about when" vs "disagreement about where", "a traditional explanation" vs "an alternative explanation". Underline the word that makes each heading different before reading. Then, for each paragraph, ask which of the pair fits its specific focus.

questions.evidence: One of the main questions is when it happened.
questions.explanation: Heading v is a detail trap: the German burial is only an example, and it is not claimed to be the oldest ever found.

questions.evidence: Where domestication took place is equally disputed.
questions.explanation: The paired headings iv and i differ only in "timing" vs "location".

questions.evidence: The traditional explanation ... Many researchers now consider this unlikely.
questions.explanation: "Traditional" = "long-established", and "consider this unlikely" = "doubts". Heading x is too narrow: danger is only one reason given.

questions.evidence: An alternative view is that wolves largely domesticated themselves.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: they had also begun to show physical changes ... even though they had been selected only for behaviour.
questions.explanation: Heading ix is not supported, because the paragraph never compares foxes with wolves as pets.

questions.evidence: the relationship between dogs and humans has had profound effects on both ... shaped the dog's mind as well as its body.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

lesson.title: Headings phrased as problems, causes and solutions
lesson.text: In problem-solution passages, headings are often abstract: "an underestimated threat", "the principal source", "technical remedies", "a change in approach". Decide which of these the paragraph mainly provides. A paragraph that mentions a cause briefly but spends most of its length on solutions is a solutions paragraph.

questions.evidence: often treated as a mere nuisance ... this view is mistaken.
questions.explanation: This is a problem paragraph that identifies an underestimated risk.

questions.evidence: disturbed sleep ... heart disease ... affect their reading and memory.
questions.explanation: The paragraph covers effects on both the body and the mind.

questions.evidence: Road traffic is by far the largest source ... two main sources: engines ... and ... tyres.
questions.explanation: Heading ii contradicts the paragraph: electric cars will make "little difference on faster roads".

questions.evidence: Special road surfaces ... though they wear out faster ... Noise barriers ... insulated windows.
questions.explanation: The paragraph presents solutions and one limitation. Heading x is a detail trap, because barriers are mentioned but their cost is not.

questions.evidence: Planning decisions matter ... bedrooms can be placed on the quiet side.
questions.explanation: This paragraph is about planning around people's needs.

questions.evidence: the goal should not simply be to reduce noise, but to improve 'soundscapes'.
questions.explanation: This describes a change in approach.

questions.evidence: noise has received less attention from governments ... It is invisible, leaves no trace.
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives the reasons for official neglect.

lesson.title: The main idea may come last
lesson.text: In some paragraphs, the writer builds up examples and details and only states the main point in the final sentence, often introduced by thus, so, in other words, this shows that. If the first sentence seems too narrow to summarise the paragraph, read the last sentence carefully.

questions.evidence: They expressed ideas about the world and a society's place within it.
questions.explanation: The main idea comes at the end. Heading x is a trap, because the passage never calls any map "the first".

questions.evidence: His work was largely forgotten in Western Europe ... but was preserved ... and became highly influential when it was rediscovered.
questions.explanation: The paragraph describes a classical foundation that was lost and recovered.

questions.evidence: Every map projection, in other words, involves choices about what to preserve and what to sacrifice.
questions.explanation: The final sentence states the main point. Heading vi is a detail trap based on one example.

questions.evidence: Accurate mapping of whole countries became possible only with systematic surveys.
questions.explanation: Heading ix is not supported, because nothing is said about sailors distrusting maps.

questions.evidence: aerial photography and then satellite imagery transformed map-making.
questions.explanation: This paragraph is about viewing the Earth from above.

questions.evidence: Maps, then, reflect the interests and assumptions of those who make them.
questions.explanation: The concluding sentence gives the main idea.

questions.evidence: The long history of maps suggests that these questions of choice and influence are not new, even if the technology is.
questions.explanation: The paragraph combines new technology with concerns that are not new.

lesson.title: Two paragraphs on the same topic
lesson.text: Some passages have two neighbouring paragraphs that discuss the same subject from different angles, for example the environmental impact of production and the environmental impact of disposal. The headings will be similarly paired. Identify what distinguishes each paragraph's focus: stage, group affected, time period or type of response.

questions.evidence: design, manufacture and deliver new styles ... in a matter of weeks.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: buys considerably more items ... but keeps each item for a much shorter time.
questions.explanation: The paragraph's main outcome is buying more and keeping less.

questions.evidence: The environmental costs begin long before the clothes reach the shops.
questions.explanation: This is the production stage. Heading v is not supported, because both cotton and polyester are shown to have costs.

questions.evidence: Further problems arise once clothes are discarded.
questions.explanation: This is the disposal stage, which is the paired heading to viii. Heading ix is a detail trap about charity.

questions.evidence: working conditions ... long hours for low wages ... safety standards.
questions.explanation: This paragraph is about the human cost.

questions.evidence: alternative ways of buying and using clothes have become more popular ... However, recycling ... remains technically difficult.
questions.explanation: The paragraph describes new habits and their limits.

questions.evidence: Some governments are now considering or introducing regulations ... voluntary efforts by companies have so far had limited effect.
questions.explanation: This matches official action supplementing voluntary efforts.

lesson.title: Chronological passages with thematic headings
lesson.text: History passages move through time, but headings often describe the significance of each stage rather than its date: "a technique that made glass widely available", "a flat surface without grinding". Don't look for dates in the headings. Ask instead: "What changed at this stage, and why did it matter?"

questions.evidence: Glass occurs in nature ... Manufactured glass ... remained a rare and valuable material.
questions.explanation: The paragraph moves from natural glass to a rare manufactured product.

questions.evidence: Glassblowing allowed vessels ... to be produced quickly and cheaply ... had become common.
questions.explanation: Heading viii is not supported, because Roman homes are not discussed.

questions.evidence: Making flat glass for windows was a greater challenge ... For centuries.
questions.explanation: "For centuries" = "persistent". Heading ix is a detail trap: mirrors are mentioned only as one use.

questions.evidence: smooth, flat surfaces on both sides, requiring no grinding or polishing. The process was cheaper.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: opening up the very small and the very distant to human observation ... optical fibres ... backbone of the internet.
questions.explanation: The paragraph covers both observation and communication.

questions.evidence: in principle, one of the most recyclable materials ... In practice, recycling rates vary.
questions.explanation: This contrasts potential with practice.

lesson.title: Research paragraphs — question, method or conclusion?
lesson.text: In research-based passages, headings often describe the role of a paragraph within the investigation: "an ancient technique", "a comparison of brains", "training ordinary people", "limits of the method". Identify whether each paragraph introduces a question, describes a study, reports a result or evaluates it.

questions.evidence: feats that seem almost impossible ... the explanation lies mainly in technique.
questions.explanation: The paragraph introduces remarkable performances and their surprising explanation.

questions.evidence: known for more than two thousand years ... Simonides ... the 'method of loci'.
questions.explanation: Heading x is a detail trap: the tragedy is the story, not the paragraph's main idea, which is the technique.

questions.evidence: gradually fell out of use in education.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: no significant differences in the structure ... What distinguished them was the way they used their brains.
questions.explanation: This is the result of the study.

questions.evidence: Volunteers with no previous experience ... could remember more than twice as many words.
questions.explanation: This is evidence that anyone can learn the skill.

questions.evidence: less useful for understanding complex ideas or developing skills.
questions.explanation: Heading viii contradicts the paragraph, since champions "forget names ... just like everyone else".

questions.evidence: might help students ... although most researchers emphasise that memorisation is only one part of learning.
questions.explanation: This describes possible uses in schools, with caution.

lesson.title: Headings that are true of the passage but not of the paragraph
lesson.text: A tempting distractor may describe something that is true somewhere in the passage, but not in the paragraph you are working on. Before you choose a heading, check that the paragraph itself develops that idea. It is not enough for the passage as a whole to mention it.

questions.evidence: The name ... describes not one road but a shifting network.
questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that the name is misleading.

questions.evidence: silk was only one of many commodities.
questions.explanation: Heading viii is a detail trap: the secret of silk is mentioned in only one clause.

questions.evidence: Ideas travelled as readily as goods ... Technologies moved as well.
questions.explanation: Beliefs and inventions are the paragraph's subject. Heading ix is too narrow, since monks are one example, and they carried religion rather than trade.

questions.evidence: Perhaps the most serious danger, however, was invisible.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: The prosperity of the routes depended heavily on political conditions.
questions.explanation: "Stability and conflict" corresponds to "controlled ... relatively safe" and "collapsed or went to war".

questions.evidence: The sea routes ... became dominant.
questions.explanation: Heading x is a keyword trap: camels are mentioned only in a comparison, and nothing says they were ideal.

questions.evidence: the idea of the Silk Road has been revived in a new form.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

lesson.title: Separate "story" details from the main point
lesson.text: History passages often include anecdotes, legends or colourful stories. These are memorable, so headings often mention them as distractors. Ask whether the story is the paragraph's main idea, or only an illustration of a larger point, such as "tea becomes part of culture" or "production moves to new regions".

questions.evidence: tea was being drunk in China at least two thousand years ago ... a scholar named Lu Yu wrote a book describing in detail how tea should be grown, prepared and served.
questions.explanation: Heading viii is a story trap: the legend illustrates the start of the paragraph but is not its main point.

questions.evidence: associated with meditation ... developed into a highly formal ceremony.
questions.explanation: This describes a spiritual and ceremonial role.

questions.evidence: At first it was an expensive novelty ... By the nineteenth century, tea had become the national drink.
questions.explanation: This traces tea's path from luxury to national habit.

questions.evidence: large quantities of silver flowed out of the country ... consequences that led to serious conflict.
questions.explanation: This describes the trade imbalance and its consequences.

questions.evidence: To reduce their dependence on China, the British began to grow tea in their colonies.
questions.explanation: Heading ix is a detail trap: working conditions appear in one clause only.

questions.evidence: Whether or not this story is accurate, tea bags became increasingly popular.
questions.explanation: "Perhaps by accident" matches the uncertain story.

questions.evidence: Its forms vary enormously ... each of which has adapted it.
questions.explanation: Heading x is not supported, because health is never compared.

lesson.title: Hard Matching Headings — implicit main ideas and argumentative structure
lesson.text:
In Hard passages:

the main idea is often implicit, spread across the paragraph rather than stated in one sentence;

headings are abstract and describe the paragraph's role in the argument, for example "a proposed explanation", "evidence that complicates it", "an objection", "a middle position"; distractors include headings that are true but too narrow, or that describe a different stage of the argument.

Strategy: for each paragraph, write two notes: its topic ("face symmetry") and its function ("evidence for the theory"). Choose the heading that fits both.

questions.evidence: Philosophers have debated ... generally treating beauty as a matter of culture ... some researchers have proposed a different kind of answer.
questions.explanation: The paragraph introduces an alternative approach. Heading xi is a detail trap: philosophers are mentioned only as background.

questions.evidence: a widespread preference for scenes resembling open grassland ... this reflects the savanna environments.
questions.explanation: This covers both the topic (landscape preference) and the function (a possible origin). Heading viii is a detail trap.

questions.evidence: symmetry and averageness may signal good health.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: relied on participants who were already familiar ... connection ... has proved weaker ... difficult to test.
questions.explanation: These are problems of both method and evidence. Heading x contradicts the paragraph's function, which is criticism, not proof.

questions.evidence: An evolutionary explanation that predicts universal preferences seems poorly suited to account for such diversity.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: Evolution ... may have provided ... general tendencies ... which culture then shapes.
questions.explanation: The paragraph proposes that biology and culture interact.

questions.evidence: Why should people value works of art that are deliberately difficult ... Why do tastes change so quickly.
questions.explanation: Heading ix is too narrow, since fashion change is only one of the unanswered questions.

lesson.title: Paragraphs that contain a turn
lesson.text: A Hard paragraph may begin with one position and then qualify or overturn it. The heading must capture the whole movement of the paragraph, not just its first half. Look for headings that combine two ideas ("success, with limitations", "a finding and its puzzling implication"), and test whether both halves appear in the paragraph.

questions.evidence: a practical tool for identifying children who needed support. He warned against treating its results as a measure of a fixed, inborn quantity.
questions.explanation: The heading captures both halves of the paragraph.

questions.evidence: His warnings were widely ignored ... in the United States ... to support discriminatory policies.
questions.explanation: "New setting" = the United States. Heading x is too narrow, since the army is only one example.

questions.evidence: Despite this troubling history, intelligence tests have proved to be among the most reliable measures.
questions.explanation: The paragraph turns on "despite", which the heading reflects in "despite an uncomfortable past".

questions.evidence: average scores ... had been rising steadily ... attributed to factors including better nutrition.
questions.explanation: This covers both the rise and its causes. Heading viii is a detail trap about the average being set at 100.

questions.evidence: the tests measure not a single fixed ability but a set of skills.
questions.explanation: This is a reassessment of what the tests measure. Heading ix contradicts the paragraph's argument.

questions.evidence: very popular among teachers ... criticised it for lacking supporting evidence.
questions.explanation: Heading xi is too narrow, since teachers' views are only part of the paragraph.

questions.evidence: Binet's original caution ... appears ... to have been well founded.
questions.explanation: "Well founded" = "vindicated".

lesson.title: Experiments with surprising results
lesson.text: Hard passages may describe an experiment whose results contradict expectations. The paragraph's main idea is then the surprise, not the method. Headings may express this as "a counter-intuitive finding" or "an outcome contrary to prediction". Separate paragraphs describing the method, the result and the interpretation carefully, because headings will target each.

questions.evidence: Increasingly, however, researchers have drawn attention to a less visible factor: trust. In societies where people generally trust one another, transactions are easier.
questions.explanation: "Less visible" = "often overlooked".

questions.evidence: the more successful regions tended to have long traditions of civic participation ... over centuries.
questions.explanation: Heading xi is too broad and misses the paragraph's explanatory point.

questions.evidence: Such surveys, however, measure what people say, not necessarily how they behave.
questions.explanation: The main idea follows "however". Heading viii is not supported: the Nordic countries report high trust, but the paragraph says nothing about their honesty.

questions.evidence: researchers 'lost' thousands of wallets ... recorded how many were returned.
questions.explanation: This paragraph describes the method and predictions. Heading ix is a detail trap.

questions.evidence: The results showed the opposite.
questions.explanation: This is the surprising result. Heading x misreads the paragraph, which is about the finding, not about economists.

questions.evidence: influenced by the quality of institutions ... Inequality also appears to matter ... easier to destroy than to create.
questions.explanation: This describes the conditions that strengthen or weaken trust.

questions.evidence: None of this means that more trust is always better. Excessive trust can make people vulnerable.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

lesson.title: Debate passages — distinguishing sides and stages
lesson.text: Passages about controversial issues move between the case for, the case against, uncertainty and governance. Headings often use evaluative words ("the economic argument", "ecological unknowns", "a regulatory gap"). Several paragraphs may mention environmental issues; decide whether each is presenting a risk, a lack of knowledge, a counter-argument or a proposal.

questions.evidence: They form extremely slowly ... The nodules contain valuable metals.
questions.explanation: Heading x is a keyword trap based on the shark's tooth detail.

questions.evidence: could supply these metals without some of the problems associated with mining on land.
questions.explanation: This is the case for deep-sea mining.

questions.evidence: Many of these animals live attached to the nodules themselves ... Removing the nodules would remove their habitat.
questions.explanation: This describes a risk to the immediate living surface. Heading ix is too narrow, and "fish" is inaccurate.

questions.evidence: Beyond the areas directly mined ... clouds of sediment that could spread over large distances.
questions.explanation: This describes a risk beyond the site, the pair to heading ii.

questions.evidence: The underlying difficulty is the lack of knowledge ... it is difficult to predict the consequences.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: has not agreed on final rules ... some countries pressing for mining ... others ... calling for a pause.
questions.explanation: Heading xi is not supported, because the companies call for a pause but are not said to have left the sector.

questions.evidence: Critics of deep-sea mining also question whether it is necessary ... recycling ... could supply a significant proportion.
questions.explanation: This questions the demand for new supplies.

lesson.title: Theories, tests and puzzles
lesson.text: Scientific-debate passages usually follow a pattern: early theories → a decisive source of evidence → a leading theory → a problem with it → proposed solutions → what remains unknown. Headings mirror these stages using abstract nouns ("a new source of data", "an unexpected similarity", "attempts at reconciliation"). Label each paragraph's stage before looking at the headings, then match.

questions.evidence: three main ideas were in circulation ... none could be decisively tested with the evidence then available.
questions.explanation: This is the early-theories stage.

questions.evidence: The samples revealed ... These findings posed serious difficulties for all three existing theories.
questions.explanation: This is the decisive evidence. Heading xi is a detail trap.

questions.evidence: a body roughly the size of Mars had collided ... could explain why the Moon has relatively little iron ... and why it was once molten.
questions.explanation: This is the leading theory. Heading x is too narrow, since size is a single detail.

questions.evidence: The giant impact theory, however, soon faced a problem ... the isotopic compositions of the Earth and Moon are almost identical.
questions.explanation: "Almost identical" = "resemblance".

questions.evidence: several ways of resolving this puzzle ... each requires particular conditions.
questions.explanation: These are proposed solutions.

questions.evidence: a series of smaller ones, each producing a small moon.
questions.explanation: "Series" = "repeated events".

questions.evidence: New evidence may help ... Samples from parts of the Moon not visited ... Improved computer models.
questions.explanation: This describes what remains to be learned.

lesson.title: Final review — the full Matching Headings method

questions.evidence: one of the most remote inhabited places ... How a small population ... managed to carve and move such enormous figures has fascinated visitors.
questions.explanation: Heading viii is a detail trap, and xi is not developed in the paragraph.

questions.evidence: the island's history was widely presented as a cautionary tale ... cleared their forests ... collapse.
questions.explanation: Heading ix is a detail within the narrative, not its main idea.

questions.evidence: rats ... may have played a major role.
questions.explanation: This introduces another possible cause of forest loss.

questions.evidence: ingenious farming techniques ... relatively few injuries ... remained relatively stable.
questions.explanation: The paragraph shows adaptation and stability.

questions.evidence: the most catastrophic changes came after European contact ... diseases ... raiders.
questions.explanation: This describes destruction brought from outside the island.

questions.evidence: Experiments by archaeologists have shown that replicas ... can be 'walked'.
questions.explanation: This is experimental evidence on the practical question of moving the statues. Heading x is not supported.

questions.evidence: it offers a different lesson altogether ... one that adapted resourcefully.
questions.explanation: The paragraph draws a new lesson from the revised history.

lesson.title: One paragraph per person
lesson.text: In easy sets, each person is usually described mainly in one paragraph. Locate each person's paragraph first, then match statements by reading that paragraph carefully. Watch for statements that paraphrase dates ("a few weeks after the other team"), and details such as survival vs death.

questions.q: changed his destination without announcing it publicly
questions.evidence: changed his plans secretly.
questions.explanation: "Secretly" = "without announcing it publicly".

questions.q: reached the Pole several weeks after a rival
questions.evidence: reached the Pole in January 1912, about five weeks after Amundsen.
questions.explanation: "Five weeks" = "several weeks".

questions.q: led an expedition in which no one died, despite losing the ship
questions.evidence: His ship ... was eventually crushed ... every member of the expedition survived.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: gave priority to science rather than to reaching the Pole
questions.evidence: focused on scientific research rather than on reaching the Pole.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: did not identify what he saw as a continent
questions.evidence: he himself did not describe it as a continent.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: learned methods from peoples living in cold northern regions
questions.evidence: Drawing on experience gained from Arctic peoples.
questions.explanation: B is used twice.

questions.q: abandoned an earlier attempt to reach the Pole to protect his team
questions.evidence: had earlier come within about 180 kilometres of the Pole, turning back to save his men's lives.
questions.explanation: D is used twice.

lesson.title: Matching characteristics to things
lesson.text: Features need not be people. Here they are types of energy. The statements describe characteristics such as advantages, disadvantages and requirements. Several energy types share some features (for example, several depend on the weather). Look for the detail that makes each statement fit only one source.

questions.q: It may require people to leave their homes.
questions.evidence: Large dams ... flood valleys, which may force communities to move.
questions.explanation: "Force communities to move" = "require people to leave their homes".

questions.q: Its output can be forecast far into the future.
questions.evidence: the timing and strength of tides can be calculated years in advance.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: they have no moving parts.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: It is currently the largest renewable source of electricity.
questions.evidence: currently the largest source of renewable electricity worldwide.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: It is mainly used where there is volcanic activity.
questions.evidence: limited mainly to regions with volcanic activity.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Some people dislike its effect on the appearance of the countryside.
questions.evidence: some people object to turbines on land because of their visual impact on the landscape.
questions.explanation: "Visual impact on the landscape" = "effect on the appearance of the countryside".

questions.q: Its output can be increased when more electricity is needed.
questions.evidence: its output can be controlled: operators can release more water when demand is high.
questions.explanation: C is used three times.

questions.q: It is available at all times of day and in all weathers.
questions.evidence: provides a constant supply of energy regardless of weather or time of day.
questions.explanation: Tidal power (E) is predictable but not constant, which makes E a trap.

lesson.title: "First" and "achievements"
lesson.text: Statements in history passages often describe achievements: the first to..., the earliest..., demonstrated publicly..., died while.... Several pioneers may have "firsts", but each first is different (first balloon flight vs first powered flight). Match the exact achievement, not just the idea of being first.

questions.q: made a flight in front of a large audience and official witnesses
questions.evidence: made a powered flight in Paris in 1906, before a large crowd and official observers.
questions.explanation: The Wright brothers (D) had few witnesses, which makes D a trap.

questions.q: described the different forces affecting a flying machine
questions.evidence: he identified the separate forces that act on a flying machine.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: worked in a business unrelated to flying machines, making paper
questions.evidence: who ran a paper-making business.
questions.explanation: The Wright brothers ran a bicycle business, so the word "paper" identifies A.

questions.q: identified control as the main difficulty to be solved
questions.evidence: the key problem was not lift or power but control.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: died as a result of a flying accident
questions.evidence: he crashed after his glider lost lift, and died the following day.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: produced a flying machine that could not be directed
questions.evidence: The balloon, however, could not be steered.
questions.explanation: "Steered" = "directed". A is used twice.

questions.q: made a design freely available to others
questions.evidence: deliberately did not patent it, making the plans freely available.
questions.explanation: E is used twice.

lesson.title: Features in a comparison passage
lesson.text: When a passage compares several places or organisations, each paragraph usually describes one. But the final paragraph often compares them directly ("only Lindholm...", "unlike the others..."). Include these comparison sentences in your search, because they can contain answers.

questions.q: A local newspaper opposed the city's policy.
questions.evidence: a local newspaper campaigned against it.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Traffic increased in areas surrounding the part of the city that was changed.
questions.evidence: traffic on the surrounding roads increased.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: A single price was introduced for all journeys of one type.
questions.evidence: introduced a simple flat fare for all journeys.
questions.explanation: "Flat fare" = "a single price".

questions.q: Health surveys found an improvement in residents' fitness.
questions.evidence: only Belvale recorded a significant improvement in the physical fitness of its residents.
questions.explanation: This answer is in the final comparison paragraph, not in Belvale's own paragraph.

questions.q: Concerns from businesses turned out to be largely unfounded.
questions.evidence: Some shopkeepers initially complained ... but surveys later suggested that most had not lost trade.
questions.explanation: "Most had not lost trade" = the concerns were "largely unfounded".

questions.q: A scheme was especially popular with visitors and students.
questions.evidence: bicycle-sharing scheme, which proved particularly popular with students and tourists.
questions.explanation: "Tourists" = "visitors".

questions.q: Money raised by the policy was spent on public transport.
questions.evidence: the revenue was used to improve public transport.
questions.explanation: The same point is repeated in paragraph F.

lesson.title: Distinguishing features with similar details
lesson.text: When several features share a detail (for example, several scripts were deciphered, or several used pictures), the statement will contain an extra detail that belongs to only one. Look for that distinguishing detail: still in use today, only consonants, written on clay, deciphered recently.

questions.q: It was originally developed to keep economic records.
questions.evidence: It began as a system for recording goods and payments.
questions.explanation: "Goods and payments" = "economic records".

questions.evidence: each representing a single consonant sound. Vowels were not written.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: It has been in use without interruption from ancient times until now.
questions.evidence: the Chinese writing system is directly descended from this early script. It is therefore the oldest writing system in continuous use today.
questions.explanation: "In continuous use" = "used without interruption". The Phoenician script (E) was adapted into new alphabets rather than continuing in use, so E is a trap.

questions.q: Most of the books written in it were deliberately destroyed.
questions.evidence: Most Maya books were destroyed by Spanish authorities.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: A multilingual inscription was the key to understanding it.
questions.evidence: a stone inscribed with the same text in three scripts ... as a key.
questions.explanation: "Three scripts" = "multilingual".

questions.q: It was used to ask questions about future events.
questions.evidence: They record questions put to ancestors or spirits, for example about harvests, weather or military campaigns.
questions.explanation: C is used twice.

questions.q: It was easier to learn than many other scripts because it had few signs.
questions.evidence: far easier to learn than scripts with hundreds of signs.
questions.explanation: E is used twice.

lesson.title: Features that are animals
lesson.text: When the features are animals or species, statements describe strategies, behaviours or physical characteristics. Several animals may share a general strategy (avoiding the cold), but each uses a specific method. Match the method, not the general goal.

questions.q: It produces young during the winter.
questions.evidence: females give birth to cubs during the winter while still in the den.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Its body contains a substance that protects it from ice damage.
questions.evidence: High concentrations of sugar in its cells prevent them from being damaged by ice.
questions.explanation: Sugar is the protective substance.

questions.q: It helps new trees to grow.
questions.evidence: those that are forgotten may grow into new trees.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Its body shape helps it travel over soft snow.
questions.evidence: Its large hind feet act like snowshoes.
questions.explanation: "Large hind feet" = "body shape".

questions.q: Its winter strategy involves no drop in activity at all, because it leaves the cold region.
questions.evidence: The Arctic tern avoids winter altogether.
questions.explanation: Squirrels (D) remain active but stay in the cold, so D is a trap.

questions.q: It may become easier for predators to see because of a change in climate.
questions.evidence: as winters become shorter, some hares turn white before snow has fallen, making them more visible.
questions.explanation: E is used twice.

questions.q: It can be woken from its winter state fairly easily.
questions.evidence: their body temperature drops only a few degrees, which allows them to wake relatively quickly.
questions.explanation: B is used twice.

lesson.title: Matching theories and their critics
lesson.text: When features are theories or researchers, statements may describe a claim, a piece of supporting evidence or a criticism. Be careful: a criticism of Theory A may be made by the supporters of Theory B. The question may ask which theory was criticised, not who made the criticism. Read each statement's grammar carefully ("a theory that was criticised for..." vs "a researcher who criticised...").

questions.q: proposed that dreams have no concealed meaning because they arise from random brain signals
questions.evidence: dreams begin with random signals ... dreams have no hidden meaning.
questions.explanation: This directly contrasts with Freud's view (A), which makes A a trap.

questions.q: was criticised for putting forward a theory that could not be tested
questions.evidence: criticised them for being impossible to test scientifically.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: found that dreams generally reflect everyday concerns
questions.evidence: dreams mostly concern the people, activities and concerns that occupy the dreamer when awake.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: suggested that dreams helped early humans survive
questions.evidence: improving their chances of survival.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: noted that people exposed to real danger dream more about threats
questions.evidence: people who have experienced real dangers tend to dream about threats more often.
questions.explanation: C is used twice.

questions.q: described findings from an experiment involving a nap
questions.evidence: people who learned to find their way through a virtual maze and then took a nap.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: was criticised for failing to explain the coherent storylines of many dreams
questions.evidence: Critics argued that the theory could not explain why dreams so often contain coherent stories.
questions.explanation: The question asks which theory was criticised, not who criticised it. B is used twice.

questions.q: suggested that dreams might have no particular purpose
questions.evidence: dreams may not have any special function at all.
questions.explanation: E is used twice.

lesson.title: Arguments that overlap
lesson.text: Scholars often agree on some points and disagree on others. Two historians may both mention coal, but one argues that it was decisive while another treats it as secondary. Statements test these distinctions. For each feature, note: main cause proposed, key evidence, and what they reject.

questions.q: argued that the relative cost of labour and fuel made new machines worthwhile
questions.evidence: wages were unusually high ... while energy ... was unusually cheap. This combination made it profitable ... to invest in machines.
questions.explanation: This is Allen's price argument.

questions.q: compared Britain with a region outside Europe
questions.evidence: comparing Britain with the most advanced regions of China.
questions.explanation: China is a region outside Europe.

questions.q: emphasised changes in the social status of business people
questions.evidence: people who made money through trade ... came to be treated with new respect.
questions.explanation: "Respect" = "social status".

questions.q: had his argument questioned on the grounds that the relevant conditions already existed earlier
questions.evidence: Critics have questioned whether these changes were as significant ... noting that property rights were already fairly secure in England before this period.
questions.explanation: The criticism is that the conditions already existed.

questions.q: accepted the importance of economic incentives but considered them insufficient
questions.evidence: Mokyr does not deny that prices mattered, but he argues that economic incentives alone cannot explain ...
questions.explanation: This is a partial acceptance, and it distinguishes Mokyr from Allen (A), who treats prices as central.

questions.q: argued that material factors were less important than changing attitudes
questions.evidence: was more important than material factors such as coal or capital.
questions.explanation: D is used twice.

questions.q: highlighted resources obtained from overseas territories
questions.evidence: access to the land and resources of the Americas.
questions.explanation: C is used twice.

questions.q: stressed the importance of the free exchange of practical knowledge
questions.evidence: practical, useful knowledge was valued and widely shared.
questions.explanation: B is used twice.

lesson.title: Ideas vs consequences vs reactions
lesson.text: For each person, a passage may describe their ideas, what happened when those ideas were applied, and how others reacted. A statement about the consequences of Le Corbusier's ideas matches Le Corbusier, even if the consequences are described in a sentence about later architects. Also watch for one person reacting against another. The statement may describe the reaction (matching the critic) or the thing reacted against (matching the original thinker).

questions.q: proposed that the benefit from rising land prices should go to the community
questions.evidence: Land would be owned collectively, so that rising land values would benefit the community.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: considered harm to residents an acceptable consequence of progress
questions.evidence: Moses believed that such costs were a necessary price of modernisation.
questions.explanation: "Modernisation" = "progress".

questions.evidence: Jacobs led a successful campaign against a highway Moses planned.
questions.explanation: The statement describes the opposition, so it matches Jacobs. The highway plan itself was Moses's (C), which makes C a trap.

questions.q: based recommendations on systematic observation of how people used public spaces
questions.evidence: Through careful observation – counting pedestrians, recording where people sat.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: proposed keeping different city activities apart
questions.evidence: Different activities – living, working, leisure – would be separated into distinct zones.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: inspired projects, some of which were later pulled down
questions.evidence: many housing projects ... were built on principles inspired by his ideas ... in several cities they were demolished.
questions.explanation: "Pulled down" = "demolished". B is used twice.

questions.q: argued that mixed uses and busy streets make neighbourhoods successful
questions.evidence: a mixture of homes, shops and workplaces ... busy streets.
questions.explanation: D is used twice.

questions.q: proposed towns of restricted size surrounded by countryside
questions.evidence: a planned town of limited size, surrounded by a permanent belt of countryside.
questions.explanation: A is used twice.

lesson.title: Technical features and problems solved
lesson.text: When features are instruments or technologies, statements often describe the problem each one solved or a limitation it had. Make a quick table for each feature: what it used, what it solved, what problem it had. Several technologies may share a general purpose, such as seeing further, but each solved a specific problem.

questions.q: It works by linking instruments in different locations.
questions.evidence: a network of radio telescopes across several continents, whose observations were combined.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Its observations challenged a long-held view of the universe.
questions.evidence: His observations provided powerful evidence against the old belief that everything in the heavens revolved around the Earth.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: It was developed following an investigation into a practical communication problem.
questions.evidence: investigating sources of interference affecting radio communications ... accidental discovery.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: A construction fault had to be corrected after it began operating.
questions.evidence: its main mirror had been ground to a slightly incorrect shape ... astronauts installed corrective equipment.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: It avoided a problem of coloured edges around images.
questions.evidence: Newton's reflecting telescope avoided the problem of coloured fringes.
questions.explanation: A is the telescope that had this problem, so A is a trap.

questions.q: It can observe objects concealed by dust.
questions.evidence: can detect objects hidden behind clouds of dust.
questions.explanation: C is used twice.

questions.q: Its design is used in most of today's largest optical telescopes.
questions.evidence: nearly all of the world's largest optical telescopes today use mirrors.
questions.explanation: B is used twice.

lesson.title: Features defined by contrast
lesson.text: When a passage describes methods that developed as reactions to one another, each method is often defined by what it rejected as well as by what it did. A statement such as "avoided the use of the learner's first language" could match a method whose paragraph says "unlike the previous method, teachers never translated". Read the contrast sentences carefully.

questions.q: It was originally used for teaching classical languages.
questions.evidence: Originally used for teaching Latin and Ancient Greek.
questions.explanation: Latin and Ancient Greek are classical languages.

questions.evidence: Teachers used only the language being taught, never translating.
questions.explanation: This is defined by contrast with grammar-translation.

questions.q: It was based on a theory that treated learning as habit formation.
questions.evidence: based on the psychological theory that learning consists of forming habits.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: It accepted mistakes that did not interfere with meaning.
questions.evidence: Errors were often tolerated if they did not prevent communication.
questions.explanation: C corrected errors immediately, which makes C a trap.

questions.q: Grammar is usually examined after learners have completed an activity.
questions.evidence: Language is studied mainly as it arises from the task, often in a later stage of the lesson.
questions.explanation: "Later stage" = "after ... completed an activity".

questions.q: Its practical use was limited by the need for highly proficient teachers.
questions.evidence: The method required teachers who were fluent speakers, which made it difficult to adopt widely.
questions.explanation: B is used twice.

questions.q: Students could produce patterns fluently but found it hard to use language flexibly.
questions.evidence: students could repeat patterns fluently but often struggled to use the language creatively.
questions.explanation: C is used twice.

questions.q: Students often could not speak the language despite understanding its grammar.
questions.evidence: Students could often analyse complex sentences accurately, but many were unable to hold even a simple conversation.
questions.explanation: A is used twice.

lesson.title: Collaborators and rivals
lesson.text: When a paragraph mentions more than one person, check who did what. Collaborators may share credit for a discovery, and the passage may attribute a later development to one of them. Rivals may be described together while taking opposite approaches. If a feature in the list is a pair (for example, "Karikó and Weissman"), statements about either person's joint work match that pair.

questions.q: produced a vaccine that was simpler to administer to large populations
questions.evidence: taken by mouth, which was cheaper and easier to give in large-scale campaigns.
questions.explanation: This distinguishes Sabin from his rival Salk (C).

questions.q: carried out a test that would not be permitted under modern standards
questions.evidence: Such an experiment would be considered unethical today.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: showed that vaccines could be made by deliberately weakening disease organisms
questions.evidence: vaccines could be produced deliberately in the laboratory, by weakening the organisms.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: found a way to reduce an unwanted reaction caused by a type of molecule
questions.evidence: modifying one of the building blocks of mRNA greatly reduced this inflammatory reaction.
questions.explanation: "Inflammatory reaction" = "unwanted reaction".

questions.q: developed a vaccine that used an inactivated virus
questions.evidence: used a virus that had been killed.
questions.explanation: "Killed" = "inactivated".

questions.q: suggested a name for the procedure to honour another scientist
questions.evidence: Pasteur proposed that the term 'vaccination' should be used ... in honour of Jenner.
questions.explanation: The statement is about Pasteur, not Jenner, which makes A a trap. B is used twice.

questions.q: had difficulty obtaining financial support for research
questions.evidence: Karikó had struggled for years to obtain funding.
questions.explanation: The paired feature E includes Karikó. E is used twice.
